lit.\u0027\u003cp\u003eA veces el objetivo n:
"

Sometimes the target cannot be disconnected directly and a functional group interconversion (FGI) is applied: for example, a 2° alcohol ⇐ ketone (reduction with NaBH₄), a ketone ⇐ 2° alcohol (oxidation), an acid ⇐ Grignard + CO₂ or ⇐ oxidation of a 1° alcohol. FGI chains steps of the synthesis together.

"
lit.\u0027\u003cp\u003eEl \u003cb\u003erendi:
"

The overall yield of a linear synthesis is the product of the yields of each step: 5 steps at 85 % give 0.85⁵ = 44 %. A convergent synthesis prepares fragments separately and joins them at the end: with the same number of steps it loses less. That is why it pays to shorten the route and be convergent.

"
lit.\u0027\u003cp\u003eLa \u003cb\u003eretro:
"

Retrosynthesis (E. J. Corey) starts from the target molecule and mentally “takes it apart” with a retrosynthetic arrow ⇒, until available starting materials are reached. Each disconnection cuts a bond where a known reaction exists that forms it. The ideal fragments are synthons (imaginary cations/anions) whose synthetic equivalent is a real reagent.

"
lit.\u0027\u003cp\u003eUn \u003cb\u003ealcoh:
"

An alcohol is disconnected at the C–C bond next to the carbinol carbon: one fragment is a carbanion (nucleophilic synthon, equivalent R–MgX) and the other a C=O (electrophilic synthon). Choose a target and a disconnection and move “Progress” to see how the fragments separate.

"
lit.\u0027\u003cp\u003eUn sintón no existe::
"

A synthon does not exist: its synthetic equivalent does. R⁻ is obtained with R–MgBr or R–Li; the ⁺C–O⁻ synthon (polarized carbonyl) is the aldehyde, ketone, ester or CO₂. There are often several possible disconnections: choose the one that gives simpler, cheaper fragments with no incompatible groups.

"
